the most relevant background variables for the psychopathology of adult psychiatric outpatients are the following: (1) personal and social characteristics of patients; (2) types of problems encountered in patient's social context, especially problems related to the social network of the patient; (3) type of precipitating events, especially events that occurred in patient's social network.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the patient himself, the patient's social context, and the patient's social problems are the most relevant background information for understanding the psychopathology of an outpatient population.

the most relevant information about the patient himself is his own personal and social history, and the most relevant information concerning his social context is the type and severity of problems he encounters.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a small number of background variables, when combined with the BPRS, can be used to identify a large portion of the systematic variance associated with the psychopathology of adult outpatients.
the patient’s own perception of the nature of his problems and the way he has been treated in the past is the most important information for the psychiatrist.
a minimum set of background information is needed to account for much systematic variance in manifest psychiatric illness in an outpatient population.
